slides.title: We started from the founders' answer, "launch", and tested the six conditions it needs; the evidence supports none of them

claims.claim: Initial hypothesis tested: “Parcelbird should launch Parcelbird Now: 9 dark stores in 3 cities, contribution-positive per order by month 18”
1. A profit pool exists, not just growth — Not met
evidence: GMV +42% a year, but −$1.90 (Zipcart) and −$3.40 (QuickBasket) per order; QuickBasket shut 36% of its cities

claims.claim: 2. A store makes money at achievable inputs — Not met
evidence: −$6.17 per order at benchmark median; −$1.76 even with every best-observed input combined

claims.claim: 3. We run stores better than the benchmark — Not shown
evidence: The pop-up was below the median on all four drivers: AOV, promotions, riders, density

claims.claim: 4. Customers stay long enough to repay their cost — Not met
evidence: $38 acquisition cost; 22% still ordering in month 3; never repaid at benchmark or pop-up economics

claims.claim: 5. The plan fits cash with 12 months of runway — Not met
evidence: $9.5M needed against $7.2M spendable above the runway floor; no new funding expected

claims.claim: 6. It beats the best other use of the cash — Not met
evidence: The software business breaks even within current cash if ARR growth stays at 34% or more

claims.claim: The hypothesis fails on every condition, so we reverse it

slides.title: Quick commerce is growing 42% a year, but both incumbents lose money on every order and one is already retreating

claims.claim: Quick commerce is growing 42% a year
evidence: US quick-commerce grocery GMV, $ billions: 2022 1.8; 2023 2.6; 2024 3.6; 2025 5.1
41.5% GMV growth a year, 2022–25

claims.claim: None of that growth has become profit
evidence: Zipcart: −26% EBITDA margin (−$310M on $1,200M), −$1.90 an order; positive only in its densest city, after a fee rise
QuickBasket: −46% margin (−$96M on $210M), −$3.40 an order; closed 4 of its 11 cities (36%)

claims.claim: Growth alone does not justify entry: "nobody owns the Midwest" may simply mean nobody has made it pay

slides.title: More volume cannot fix a store losing $6.17 per order at benchmark median: $2.67 of it goes before any site cost

claims.claim: Each order brings in $11.17 but costs $13.84 before any site cost
evidence: Waterfall (median of 14 customer sites, 2025): Goods margin 9.18; Fee 1.99; Promotions −2.04; Picking −3.10; Riders −7.40 (6.03 + 1.36583 below zero); Payment −1.30; Before site cost −2.66583
Goods margin 27% × $34 AOV; promotions 6% × $34; riders $17.75 an hour ÷ 2.4 orders = $7.40

claims.claim: Volume spreads only the $3.50 of site cost; each extra order still loses $2.67
evidence: At 900 orders a day: Before site cost −2.66583; Site cost −3.50076; After site cost −6.16659
site cost $1.15M a year ÷ 328,500 orders

claims.claim: Only a sharp rise in AOV or rider productivity turns it positive; riders alone take 81% of goods margin
evidence: two of three cities weigh rider minimum pay

slides.title: Only the founders' plan makes money; even the best-observed result on every driver at once loses $1.76 per order

claims.claim: No combination of observed inputs makes money
evidence: Before / after site fixed cost, $ per order: Columbus pop-up (actual) −6.21238 / −12.5725; Benchmark median −2.66583 / −6.16659; Best observed (all drivers) 0.493333 / −1.75716; Founders' plan 3.76857 / 2.01819
Inputs (AOV, promotions, orders per rider-hour, orders a day): pop-up $31, 12%, 2.1, 280; median $34, 6%, 2.4, 900; best $42, 6%, 3.0, 1,400; plan $45, 2%, 3.5, 1,800

claims.claim: Best observed: the best AOV ($42) and the best density (1,400 orders a day) come from different sites; combining them is already optimistic, and it still loses money
Nine stores: −$2.0M a store a year means −$18.2M for the median network and −$8.1M at best observed; only the plan's inputs give a profit, +$11.9M
Break-even AOV: with other inputs held, the median store needs $63 and the best-observed store $50, against a median of $34 and a best of $42
evidence: After site fixed cost spreads each store's $1.15M a year of rent, staff and utilities (pop-up $0.65M); both measures exclude HQ overhead, capex and marketing

slides.title: The plan must beat the best site observed on all four drivers; median AOV or rider productivity alone turns it loss-making

claims.claim: The plan needs more than the best site on every driver
evidence: AOV: $45, 7% above the best site's $42 (median $34); promotions: 2% of AOV, 4 percentage points below the best site's 6%
Riders and density: 3.5 orders per rider-hour and 1,800 orders a day, 17% and 29% above the top of the observed ranges (1.9–3.0 and 400–1,400)

claims.claim: Exposure: at the median, AOV or rider productivity alone turns the plan negative; density or promotions alone leave a thin $0.2–0.3 per order, with nothing for HQ overhead or marketing
evidence: Plan contribution per order after site fixed cost, one driver at median: Plan as proposed 2.01819; AOV $45 → $34 −0.731809; Riders 3.5 → 2.4 an hour −0.306214; Orders a day 1,800 → 900 0.26781; Promotions 2% → 6% 0.218191

claims.claim: Scale check: nine plan stores would sell $266M a year, more than QuickBasket's $210M revenue
evidence: 9 stores × 1,800 orders a day × $45 × 365 = $266M, about 5% of the 2025 US market; GMV taken as roughly equal to an operator's revenue

slides.title: No evidence yet that we run stores better: our Columbus pop-up trailed the benchmark median on every driver

claims.claim: The pop-up is our only test of a capability edge
evidence: Benchmark median: AOV $34; Promo 6%; Orders per hour 2.4; Orders a day 900; Contribution −$2.67 / −$6.17
Columbus pop-up: AOV $31; Promo 12%; Orders per hour 2.1; Orders a day 280; Contribution −$6.21 / −$12.57
Founders' plan: AOV $45; Promo 2%; Orders per hour 3.5; Orders a day 1,800; Contribution +$3.77 / +$2.02

claims.claim: The claim: "we know how to run them better than anyone"; the pop-up did worse than the median of the stores our software runs
evidence: Against the median: AOV 9% lower, promotions twice as high, 13% fewer orders per rider-hour, 69% fewer orders a day

claims.claim: Fair caveat, it was early
evidence: orders grew 18% a week, from about 178 a day to about 407 in week 6 (our estimate), but with 12% promotions and $38 CAC
Week 1 and week 6 orders: our estimate, assuming constant 18% weekly growth and a six-week average of 280 orders a day

claims.claim: Ramp-up alone does not close the gap: even at median density the store would still lose $6.17 per order (p. 5)
evidence: Pop-up site cost: $650,000 a year ÷ (280 × 365 orders) = $6.36 per order; rider cost: $17.75 ÷ 2.1 = $8.45 per order

slides.title: Customers leave before repaying a $38 acquisition cost: 44% expect to order weekly, yet only 22% still ordered in month 3

claims.claim: Buying growth destroys value: at the median every customer acquired adds to the losses; even on the plan, payback takes over a year
evidence: Columbus pop-up: −$6.21; Never; Never
Benchmark median: −$2.67; Never; Never
Best observed: +$0.49; 77 orders; 113 months (about 9 years)
Founders' plan: +$3.77; 10 orders; 15 months
Months = ($38 ÷ contribution per order) ÷ 0.68 orders a month per acquired customer (22% × 3.1); generous: no churn after month 3, contribution before any site cost

claims.claim: What customers say is not what they do
evidence: 44% of Columbus residents aged 25–39 say they would order at least weekly (n = 1,500)
22% of pop-up customers still ordering in month 3, at 3.1 orders a month
Acquisition cost per customer $38

slides.title: Copying Zipcart's $3.99 fee and near-zero promotions, at 14% less volume, leaves our median store losing $1.05 per order

claims.claim: Copying Zipcart's moves leaves our median store losing $1.05 per order
evidence: Benchmark median −6.16659; +$3.99 service fee 3.99; Promotions 6% → 1% 1.7; Volume −14%: site cost per order −0.569891; With Zipcart's moves −1.04649

claims.claim: A route may exist, but only with premium pricing at top density
evidence: Volume lost 14%: Zipcart's "+$0.40 per order" held only in its densest city, after a new $3.99 fee and promotions cut to 1%
Break-even volume 1,042: Orders a day needed at +$3.02 before site cost: 16% above today's median, 3.7 times the pop-up, same rider productivity

claims.claim: Premium pricing at top-quartile density is not where a new entrant starts, and nothing in our data shows it yet

slides.title: Even on the founders' numbers the launch breaks the one-year runway rule; adding core burn, cash runs out in month 13

claims.claim: Only $7.2M can be spent while keeping 12 months of runway; the founders need $9.5M to month 18
evidence: Cash in bank 12; Floor (12 × $0.4M) 4.8; Spendable 7.2
Spendable 7.2 vs Need to month 18 9.5; −$2.3M

claims.claim: Every reading breaks the investors' constraints
evidence: Cash out in month 13: If the $9.5M comes on top of today's core burn, with ARR growing 60%: runway falls below 12 months in month 5 (p. 13)
Left at month 18 $2.5M: If the $9.5M covers all spending: about 6 months of runway at today's burn, against the 12 required
Nine stores a year −$18.2M: A mature network at benchmark economics loses about $1.5M a month, more than our cash each year; a new round is "unlikely"

claims.claim: The floor rises once stores operate, because a higher burn needs a larger 12-month reserve; the $7.2M of headroom is therefore a ceiling

slides.title: Of the three options, only software-first meets both investor constraints and keeps a foothold in fast delivery

claims.claim: A. Launch Parcelbird Now fails every criterion
evidence: Per-order economics: No: −$6.17 at the median; positive only on plan inputs
Cash need: No: $9.5M to month 18 (plan)
12-month runway rule: No: breached in month 5; cash out in month 13
Path to profit: No: only if every driver beats the best observed
Strategic fit: No: competes with the grocers we sell to; distracts the team
Main risk: Unit economics never close; cash runs out

claims.claim: B. One permanent pilot store (Columbus) fails or only partly meets the criteria
evidence: Per-order economics: No: −$6.17 at the median; −$12.57 pop-up actual
Cash need: Partly: $0.6M capex plus about $2.0M a year of losses
12-month runway rule: No: breached in month 10
Path to profit: No: a single store cannot reach scale
Strategic fit: Partly: little new learning; pop-up and 14-site data already exist
Main risk: Losses with no route to scale

claims.claim: C. Software-first + store-based fast delivery for grocers (recommended) meets every criterion
evidence: Per-order economics: Yes: 81% gross margin on $96k contracts
Cash need: Yes: $0.8M a year of hires, phased
12-month runway rule: Yes: never below 24 months at 60% growth
Path to profit: Yes: break-even in month 26 (60% growth) or 36 (40%)
Strategic fit: Yes: meets demand already in the pipeline
Main risk: ARR growth falls below 34% a year
Runway and break-even figures come from the monthly cash model (pp. 13–15) and assume software ARR grows 60% a year unless stated

slides.title: Launching runs out of cash in month 13 and a pilot nears zero; software-first bottoms out at $5.4M, then turns cash-positive

claims.claim: Only software-first keeps the runway rule
evidence: Projected cash balance, $M, ARR +60% in all three: C. Software-first 12 at month 0, low 5.39 at month 25, 7.54 at month 36; A. Launch 12 at month 0, −0.38 at month 13, low −2.54 at month 22, 0.44 at month 36; B. Pilot 12 at month 0, low 0.16 at month 30, 0.87 at month 36

claims.claim: A. Cash out in month 13
evidence: Runway below 12 months from month 5; lowest cash −$2.5M, even in the founders' best case

claims.claim: B. Lowest cash $0.2M
evidence: Runway below 12 months from month 10, with no route to scale

claims.claim: C. Lowest cash $5.4M
evidence: Never below 12 months of runway; cash-positive from month 26

claims.claim: Model basis
evidence: Burn ($0.4M a month) = software opex − gross profit; opex flat apart from the $0.8M hires (B and C only); runway = cash ÷ recurring monthly burn
A: $5.4M capex at one store a month (months 1–9) plus the plan's other $4.1M spread over months 1–18, nothing after; B: $0.6M capex, then the median store's −$2.0M a year

slides.title: Software-first holds the runway rule within current cash while ARR grows at least 34% a year, just over half today's 60%

claims.claim: 34% a year is the floor
evidence: Projected cash, $M: 60% low 5.39 (month 25), 16.33 at month 48; 40% low 2.68 (months 34–35), 4.76 at month 48; 34% low 1.25 (month 40), 1.86 at month 48

claims.claim: Today's growth 60%
evidence: Break-even in month 26; lowest cash $5.4M; runway never below 24 months

claims.claim: Slower growth 40%
evidence: Break-even in month 36; lowest cash $2.7M; runway at least 18 months

claims.claim: Minimum growth 34%
evidence: Break-even in month 41; lowest cash $1.2M; runway just holds at 12 months

claims.claim: Too slow 25%
evidence: No break-even by month 48; cash runs out and the rule is breached

claims.claim: Break-even ARR
evidence: Break-even ARR = opex ÷ 81% gross margin = $8.9M ÷ 0.81 = $11.0M, against $4.1M today (p. 15)

slides.title: The pipeline supports the hires, but with no churn or win-rate data they should be phased against signed contracts

claims.claim: $11M ARR needed to break even, against $4.1M of ARR today
evidence: Opex of $8.9M a year including the $0.8M of hires, ÷ the 81% gross margin
34% growth needs about 15 net new contracts in year 1; 60% about 26
Costs must stay flat apart from the hires

claims.claim: 37 grocers in the software sales pipeline; 9 at the late stage, worth $0.86M of ARR
evidence: All 37 together are worth $3.55M of ARR at $96k a year each
Several want fast delivery from their own stores
The pack gives no churn or win rates for them

claims.claim: 28% share of the pipeline pays for the hires; about 10 contracts cover $0.8M a year
evidence: Each $96k contract earns about $78k a year of gross profit at 81%
Release the hires in two tranches against signed contracts
Hold the second tranche if growth tracks below 34%

slides.title: The recommendation survives the main uncertainties: most would make a launch worse, and software-first's risks can be managed

claims.claim: Rider minimum-pay rules (2 of 3 cities): Strengthens "don't launch"
evidence: +20% rider cost = +$1.48 per order at the median, +$1.01 on the plan
Mitigation: None needed for C; track the rules for any future re-entry
+20% is the analysis's illustrative size for the minimum-pay rules; the briefing pack gives no figure (source not verified)

claims.claim: Density in mid-size Midwest cities: Strengthens "don't launch"
evidence: Pop-up 280 a day against a median of 900; benchmark range 400–1,400
Mitigation: Trigger 2 (p. 17) tracks density across customer sites

claims.claim: Raising AOV could erode the convenience use case: Strengthens "don't launch"
evidence: The plan needs $45, against $42 best observed and $31 at the pop-up
Mitigation: Trigger 2 (p. 17)

claims.claim: A competitor claims the Midwest first: Low: first-mover status has not created profit
evidence: Incumbents are retreating (QuickBasket closed 4 cities) and lose money per order
Mitigation: Re-entry later can use our software data

claims.claim: Software growth slows below the minimum: Main risk to C
evidence: Below 34% a year, C breaches the runway rule; at 25% it runs out of cash
Mitigation: Phase hires against signed contracts; review the cost base quarterly

claims.claim: Software cost base grows faster than assumed: Delays C's break-even
evidence: The model holds opex flat apart from the $0.8M of hires
Mitigation: Board-approved opex envelope; monthly runway reporting

claims.claim: Grocers' own fast delivery competes with our customers: Upside for C
evidence: Several pipeline grocers want store-based fast delivery
Mitigation: Package store-based fast delivery as a product

slides.title: Reconsider an operator model only when our customers' sites show the economics work and the funding exists

claims.claim: Proposed re-entry triggers, reviewed quarterly from data our software already collects across the 14 customer sites, at no extra cost
evidence: 1 Site-level profit is proven: At least one customer site shows positive contribution after site cost for two consecutive quarters — Today: None: best-observed inputs give −$1.76 per order

2 The profit drivers are seen at one site at the same time: AOV of $42 or more and 3.0 or more orders per rider-hour at 1,050 or more orders a day, or a service fee that does the same job without losing more than 15% of volume — Today: No site has both; break-even with Zipcart's moves needs about 1,042 orders a day
3 Customers stay: Month-3 retention high enough to repay $38 of acquisition cost within 12 months at actual contribution — Today: 22% at 3.1 orders a month, so payback never happens at the median
4 Funding is ring-fenced: Dedicated capital that leaves the core business with 12 months of runway at all times — Today: A new round is "unlikely"; headroom is $7.2M against a $9.5M plan

slides.title: We ask the board to make four decisions in January 2027 and to review progress at an April 2027 checkpoint

claims.claim: 1 Decline the 2027 launch of Parcelbird Now (Board · January 2027)
evidence: Commit no capex to dark stores
Do not extend the pop-up (annualised loss about $1.3M)
Keep the pop-up data and cohort learning

claims.claim: 2 Approve the software scale-up (CEO · Q1 2027)
evidence: 2 engineers and 2 sales hires, $0.8M a year
Released in two tranches tied to signed late-stage contracts
Late stage: 9 grocers worth $0.86M of ARR

claims.claim: 3 Build a store-based fast-delivery offer (CTO and Sales · Q2 2027)
evidence: Package picking and rider dispatch for grocers who want fast delivery from existing stores
Test it with late-stage pipeline accounts
Gives us a share of the market's growth without running stores

claims.claim: 4 Adopt re-entry triggers and runway reporting (CFO · Q1 2027)
evidence: Quarterly dashboard of the 4 triggers from customer-site data
Monthly runway against the 12-month rule
First dashboard at the April 2027 checkpoint

claims.claim: April checkpoint: late-stage conversions, store-based pilot interest, ARR growth against the 34% minimum; if growth is below 34%, hold the second tranche

claims.claim: "Contribution per order": shown both before and after site fixed cost — does not change the answer
evidence: The founders and incumbents don't define it
No: the median is negative on both

claims.claim: Founders' $9.5M: both readings — does not change the answer
evidence: Unclear whether it includes the core $0.4M a month of burn
on top of core burn (cash out in month 13) and all-in ($2.5M left at month 18)
No: both breach the 12-month rule

normalized.recommendation: Decline the 2027 launch of Parcelbird Now (commit no capex to dark stores; do not extend the pop-up); approve the software scale-up (2 engineers and 2 sales hires, $0.8M a year, released in two tranches tied to signed late-stage contracts); build a store-based fast-delivery offer for grocers; adopt re-entry triggers and runway reporting, with an April 2027 checkpoint at which the second tranche is held if growth is below 34%.

alternatives_considered.option: A. Launch Parcelbird Now (9 dark stores, 3 cities)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected: −$6.17 per order at the median, positive only on plan inputs; $9.5M to month 18; runway rule breached in month 5, cash out in month 13; competes with the grocers we sell to; main risk: unit economics never close, cash runs out.

Rejected: −$6.17 at the median, −$12.57 pop-up actual; $0.6M capex plus about $2.0M a year of losses; runway rule breached in month 10; a single store cannot reach scale; little new learning; losses with no route to scale. Noted as not in the briefing pack.

alternatives_considered.option: C. Software-first + store-based fast delivery for grocers
alternatives_considered.treatment: Recommended: 81% gross margin on $96k contracts; $0.8M a year of hires, phased; never below 24 months of runway at 60% growth; break-even in month 26 (60%) or 36 (40%); meets demand already in the pipeline; main risk ARR growth below 34% a year.

alternatives_considered.option: Copying Zipcart's $3.99 fee and near-zero promotions
alternatives_considered.treatment: Leaves the median store losing $1.05 per order at 14% less volume; break-even needs about 1,042 orders a day; premium pricing at top-quartile density is not where a new entrant starts.

assumptions_and_uncertainties: Prepared from the board briefing pack only (synthetic benchmark data); no external research
Rider minimum-pay rules (2 of 3 cities): +20% is the analysis's illustrative size; the briefing pack gives no figure (source not verified)
Software growth slowing below 34% a year is the main risk to C; at 25% it runs out of cash
Software cost base: the pack gives burn, not opex; opex = 81% × ARR + burn, held flat apart from the $0.8M hires — optimistic for C
The pack gives no churn or win rates for pipeline grocers
Founders' $9.5M: unclear whether it includes the core $0.4M a month of burn; both readings shown
Runway = cash ÷ recurring monthly burn; one-off capex excluded from the burn (lenient)
The floor rises once stores operate; the $7.2M of headroom is therefore a ceiling
Contribution per order is not defined by founders or incumbents; shown before and after site fixed cost
GMV taken as roughly equal to an operator's revenue (scale check only)
Pop-up ramp assumed constant 18% weekly compounding; week 1 and week 6 orders are estimates
Best observed combines AOV and density from different sites, which is already optimistic
Payback months are generous: no churn after month 3, contribution before any site cost
Unit economics exclude HQ overhead, capex and marketing

normalized.extraction_notes: The deck had no images, so I had nothing to transcribe from pictures. I gave chart values as the raw series values from the text extraction, keeping their unrounded decimals. Waterfall charts on slides 5 and 10 come through as invisible 'base' series plus visible series, and I turned them into step values. On slide 5 I combined the Riders step (6.03 + 1.36583) into one figure. For the long line charts on slides 13 and 14, I summarized key points (start, low, end) instead of listing every month. On slide 8, the shading key ('Weaker'/'Stronger') wasn't extracted as a claim. Slide 2 had stray page refs and numbering, which I left out.
